meta.descriptionEn: On the evening of 21 October 1978, twenty-year-old pilot Frederick Valentich flew a Cessna 182 across Bass Strait. During the flight he told Melbourne air traffic control that a large, unknown aircraft with bright lights was orbiting above him. His engine began running roughly. Then came his last words: "It's not an aircraft." A metallic scraping sound followed, and then silence. A huge sea and air search found nothing. Was it a UFO, a pilot's illusion, or something he planned himself? We follow the radio transcript, the search, the strange cowl flap found years later, and the theories from ufologists, skeptics and investigators. Watch to the end to weigh the evidence.

articleEn: On an evening in October 1978, a pilot's voice came over the radio in the skies above Australia. He said, "It's not an aircraft." His name was Frederick Valentich, and he was only 20 years old. He was flying a small Cessna over Bass Strait.

Moments earlier, he had told the Melbourne controller that a strange aircraft was circling above him. Then his engine began to fail. After that, strange metallic scraping sounds came over the radio, and then there was complete silence. Valentich and his aircraft were never found.

So what was above him? Was an unknown object really flying alongside him, or was something else going on? What happened to the aircraft? And why was the young man headed toward King Island that evening? Even today, the reason is not fully clear.

In this story, we look at the surviving evidence: the radio conversation, the search, the investigations, and the theories that try to explain the mystery. Some say it was a UFO. Others believe it was a dangerous illusion. What is the truth? Let's start from the beginning.

articleEn: Frederick Valentich was born on 9 June 1958. His dream was a career in aviation. According to sources, this was more than a hobby: he was very enthusiastic about flying and was a member of the RAAF Air Training Corps. He applied twice to join the Royal Australian Air Force, and both times he was rejected because his educational qualifications were insufficient. He did not give up. He studied part time to become a commercial pilot.

The path was not easy. The commercial licence had five subjects, and he had failed all of them twice. His record of achievement was weak. A month before he disappeared, he had also failed three more commercial licence subjects. Failure seemed to follow him. Yet he stayed committed to his dream despite repeated obstacles, and every flight may have mattered a great deal to him.

As for experience, he had roughly 150 hours of total flying time, so he was still a fairly new pilot. He held a class-four instrument rating. This allowed him to fly at night, but only in visual meteorological conditions, meaning when weather and visibility were clear. He was not permitted to fly on instruments alone in poor visibility. This point becomes very important later. He did have permission to fly at night, and the flight on 21 October took place in the evening.

His record also included some flying incidents. Once he strayed into controlled airspace in Sydney and received a warning. The second matter was more serious: he had twice deliberately flown into cloud, and prosecution was being considered. The picture is of an enthusiastic young man with limited experience, difficulties with exams, and incidents that had drawn the attention of the authorities. We are not blaming anyone. articleEn: Bass Strait is a stretch of sea between mainland Australia and the island of Tasmania. It separates the coast of Victoria from Tasmania. It is about 250 kilometres wide and about 500 kilometres long. Its average depth is only 60 metres, which makes it fairly shallow. It is the most direct sea route between the Great Australian Bight and the Tasman Sea, and the only sea route into Port Phillip Bay.

The strait formed about 8,000 years ago, when sea levels rose at the end of the last glacial period and the old land route was flooded. Thousands of years earlier, there was no sea here but a land bridge called the Bassian Plain. Aboriginal Tasmanians reached Tasmania by this route about 40,000 years ago. It is named after the English explorer and physician George Bass, who travelled the area with Matthew Flinders in 1798 and 1799.

But the sea is dangerous as well as beautiful. Powerful currents and stormy waves from the Antarctic are well known here, and the shallow water keeps it especially rough. Many ships sank here in the 19th century, and shipwrecks along the coasts of Tasmania and Victoria number in the hundreds. Strong metal ships and modern navigation have reduced the danger considerably. Lighthouses were built to give light: Cape Otway Lighthouse was first lit in 1848, and the Cape Wickham lighthouse on the north of King Island in 1861. Cape Otway is on the Victorian coast, and King Island lies in the western part of the strait. Under the International Hydrographic Organization's definition, they are part of its western limit.

Many vessels vanished in this sea leaving no trace, or very little. This is why legends of piracy and the supernatural grew up, like those of the Bermuda Triangle. According to sources, though, the usual cause of such disappearances is a dangerous mix of wind and sea. There are also many semi-submerged rocks and reefs. In the early 19th century it was a relatively safe route for ships sailing from Europe or India to Sydney, and it saved about 1,300 kilometres.
So why did a young pilot flying at night over such a sea get into trouble? The story of his last flight comes next.

articleEn: On the evening of Saturday, 21 October 1978, 20-year-old Frederick Valentich was about to take off in a Cessna 182L, registration VH-DSJ. The Cessna 182L is a single-engine light aircraft. It was a small plane, and it was to cross Bass Strait to reach King Island. The flight was 125 nautical miles, about 232 kilometres.

Valentich had about 150 flying hours in total and held a class-four instrument rating. Under it he could fly at night, but only in visual meteorological conditions, basically conditions where he could fly by looking outside. The biggest question is why he was going to King Island. The real purpose of the flight is still unknown. He told flight officials he was going to pick up friends from King Island. He told others he was going to buy crayfish. But later investigation showed both reasons to be false.

Another thing was strange. Valentich had not told King Island Airport about his intention to land, which, according to sources, went against standard procedure. So the airport had no advance notice of his arrival. He had also had flying incidents before. Once he strayed into controlled airspace in Sydney and received a warning. The previous month he had failed three commercial licence subjects. Prosecution was being considered for twice flying deliberately into cloud.

Supporters of one theory say that even after a 30 to 45 minute trip to Cape Otway, the aircraft would still have had enough fuel to fly 800 kilometres. This belongs to the staged disappearance theory, which we will discuss in detail later. For now, we only look at the facts. In the evening, a 20-year-old pilot, who had given a reason that later proved false, was flying over Bass Strait. Then contact was made with Melbourne.

articleEn: Now comes the moment that made this story famous. At 7:06 pm, Valentich sent a radio message to Melbourne Flight Service. He reported that an unidentified aircraft was following him at 4,500 feet. He was told there was no known traffic at that level. That reply became the first big question of the story.

Valentich said he could see a large unknown aircraft that appeared lit by four bright landing lights. He could not confirm its type. But he said it had passed about 1,000 feet above him at very high speed. Then he said it was now approaching him from the east. He also said the other pilot might be deliberately playing games with him. After that he reported that the aircraft was orbiting above him. Its surface looked like shiny metal, and it had a green light.

During this time Valentich also reported engine problems. According to sources, the engine was running roughly. Valentich was only permitted to fly at night in visual conditions, and that night he was describing something he could not identify. Melbourne Flight Service asked him to identify the aircraft. In reply, Valentich said: "It's not an aircraft." After this the transmission was filled with unidentified noise, described as metallic, scraping sounds. Then all contact was lost, followed by silence. Valentich's voice was never heard again.

What was really in the sky before that silence? According to another source, the object came directly in front of his aircraft, whereas in the first source it passed overhead. Some experts believe the rough idling was caused by reduced fuel flow from G-forces during a spiral. We will look at that theory later. The same review said the steady lights seen above were probably Venus, Mars, Mercury and the star Antares. That theory comes later too. According to Brian Dunning, the conversation resembled a scene from the film Close Encounters, released less than a year earlier.

Radio transcripts of the conversation exist. In 2013, astronomer James McGaha and author Joe Nickell reviewed those transcripts and other data. These were the final moments: a pilot, and something in the sky that nobody could name. Could he be found?

articleEn: Yes, a search began. A large sea and air search was launched, which included help from ships. Valentich had given his last message to Melbourne, and now the whole system set about finding him. It included a RAAF Lockheed P-3 Orion aircraft. Eight civilian aircraft also scanned the sea's surface from the air. The search covered more than 1,000 square miles, about 2,600 square kilometres. That is a very large sea area, and finding one small light aircraft in it is like finding a needle in a haystack. But nothing was found. On 25 October 1978, the search efforts were ended without any result.

There was another angle. That night there were some reports of UFO sightings, but they were belated, meaning they came in late. The Department of Transport was sceptical of them. Some of its officials thought Valentich had become disoriented. According to them, he may have seen the reflection of his own lights in the water, or the lights of a nearby island, while the aircraft was flying upside down. This was only a guess.

Then came the official investigation. The Australian Department of Transport's investigations could not determine the cause. About Valentich, they wrote only that he was presumed fatal. That means it was officially assumed that Valentich had died, but the cause remained unknown.

Was any physical clue ever found? Yes, five years later. An engine cowl flap was found washed up on the shore of Flinders Island. A cowl flap is a part of the engine cover. This was important because it was a possible physical clue. In July 1983, the Bureau of Air Safety Investigation asked the Royal Australian Navy Research Laboratory, or RANRL for short, a question: could this cowl flap have drifted from the area where the aircraft disappeared? That is, could it have travelled through the sea? The Bureau wrote that the part came from a Cessna 182 aircraft and belonged to a particular range of serial numbers, and that range included Valentich's aircraft. This is important, but it could not explain the disappearance.

Think about it: a fragment found five years later in a very large sea. It is both a clue and a new question. The investigations did not say what was in the sky that evening. But those who believe in UFOs had a story of their own. It comes next.

articleEn: Now let's talk about ufologists, the people who study UFOs. Some of them claim this was no ordinary accident. They say either a UFO destroyed Valentich's aircraft, or abducted him. This is a claim, not an established fact. To support it, they cite reports from some people. According to them, some individuals saw an erratically moving green light in the sky. It was also said that Valentich was in a steep dive. Ufologists consider the green light important because Valentich also mentioned a green light on the radio.

But there is another side. Mount Stromlo Observatory said there was a meteorite stream that night, with ten to fifteen sightings an hour. So this could be one possible cause of the bright lights in the sky.

Now to the photographs. A group called Ground Saucer Watch, from Phoenix, Arizona, claims some photos show a fast-moving object. The photos were taken by plumber Roy Manifold on the same day. According to the claim, the object appears to rise out of the water near Cape Otway Lighthouse. According to UFO writer Jerome Clark, the group said it was a bona fide unknown flying object, surrounded by what seemed to be cloud-like vapour or exhaust. But according to the source, the photos were not clear enough to identify the object. The claim was big, but the image was not clear. Snopes editor Jordan Liles has a different opinion. He thinks the object was most likely an out-of-focus fly, or a bird passing close by.

Now let's look at the bigger picture. UFO means something seen in the sky that has not yet been identified. It does not mean an alien being. Studies show that after detailed investigation, most UFOs turn out to be ordinary objects or natural phenomena, such as aircraft, balloons, satellites, meteors, bright stars and planets. A small number remain unexplained. According to one source, fewer than ten percent of reports remain unexplained after investigation. According to Steven Novella, the cause of such reports may simply be incomplete information. Unexplained does not automatically mean alien.
So is there another explanation? Some experts believe the answer may lie in the pilot's own perception. The next part is about that.

articleEn: Now we turn to explanations that do not involve a UFO. One theory comes from the 2013 review by McGaha and Nickell. According to them, Valentich was inexperienced and may have fallen victim to a tilted horizon illusion. He tried to correct it. Remember one thing: Valentich had about 150 flying hours, and his class-four rating allowed him to fly only in visual conditions. In the attempt, the aircraft unknowingly went into a downward graveyard spiral. According to the authors, Valentich at first took this for simple orbiting. As a spiral tightens, G-forces rise. The authors say this can reduce fuel flow, and the engine could be heard idling roughly. And the steady lights seen above? According to them, they were probably the planets Venus, Mars and Mercury, along with the star Antares. By this theory, they would all behave just as Valentich described. Still, this is only a theory, not an established fact.

The second theory is Brian Dunning's. According to him, Valentich's radio conversation resembled a scene from the film Close Encounters of the Third Kind. The film had been released less than a year earlier and was popular with pilots, young people and UFO fans. Dunning guesses that Valentich may have been mimicking it as a joke, and flew the aircraft in circles to show the radar operators something. By this theory he then became disoriented by mistake and the aircraft hit the water. This too is only a guess.

The third theory is more dramatic: that Valentich staged his own disappearance. Some arguments are given in its favour. First, even after a 30 to 45 minute trip to Cape Otway, the Cessna 182 would have had enough fuel to fly 800 km. Second, conditions were excellent, yet the aircraft was never plotted on radar. This raises doubt about whether he was even near Cape Otway. Third, Melbourne police received reports at the same time of a light aircraft landing mysteriously near Cape Otway. These are arguments, not proof. Some people also raised the possibility that he harmed himself, but according to Keith Basterfield, interviews with doctors and colleagues all but ruled it out.
So which theory is true? Perhaps none has been proven. Every explanation comes with a question attached, and in the next section we will gather those questions together.

articleEn: So in the end the question is the same one we started with. What really happened to Frederick Valentich? On the evening of 21 October 1978, a 20-year-old pilot told Melbourne over the radio for the last time that it was not an aircraft. Then silence fell.

First, what is known. Valentich was never found, and the search ended without result on 25 October 1978. Only an engine cowl flap was found five years later on Flinders Island. It was part of a Cessna 182, but it does not prove what happened to the aircraft. The Department of Transport's investigation could not determine the cause. It said only that Valentich should be presumed fatal.

Now, what is not known. No solid evidence of any UFO has emerged, and the photos that were shown were not clear. On the other side, theories such as spatial disorientation, a staged disappearance and an imitation of Close Encounters are also only suggestions. None has been proven.

There is also a lesson in this story. Valentich had about 150 hours of experience, and his instrument rating allowed him to fly at night only in visual conditions. According to McGaha and Nickell, an inexperienced pilot can be fooled in such circumstances. That is their theory, but it is certainly a message of caution for pilots.

Culturally, the incident is still counted among Australia's most famous UFO cases. It took place over Bass Strait. A family lost their son, and to this day they have not received a complete answer. shorts.titleEn: "It's Not an Aircraft": The Last Radio Call Over Bass Strait
shorts.text: کیا ایک pilot کی آخری آواز راز ہے؟ 21 October 1978 کی شام، 20 سال کا Frederick Valentich ایک Cessna جہاز میں Bass Strait کے اوپر تھا۔ شام 7:06 بجے اس نے Melbourne Flight Service کو radio پر بتایا کہ ایک unidentified aircraft 4,500 feet پر اس کا پیچھا کر رہا ہے۔ جواب ملا کہ اس level پر کوئی known traffic نہیں ہے۔ Valentich نے کہا کہ اسے ایک بڑا جہاز نظر آ رہا ہے، جو چار bright landing lights سے روشن ہے۔ وہ تقریباً 1,000 feet اوپر سے بہت تیز رفتار سے گزرا۔ پھر اس نے engine کی خرابی کا بتایا۔ آخر میں اس نے کہا: It's not an aircraft۔ اس کے بعد radio پر metallic scraping آوازیں آئیں، اور پھر مکمل خاموشی۔ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: Kya ek pilot ki aakhri awaz raaz hai? 21 October 1978 ki sham, 20 saal ka Frederick Valentich ek Cessna jahaz mein Bass Strait ke upar tha. Sham 7:06 bajay us ne Melbourne Flight Service ko radio par bataya ke ek unidentified aircraft 4,500 feet par is ka peecha kar raha hai. Jawab mila ke is level par koi known traffic nahin hai. Valentich ne kaha ke use ek bara jahaz nazar aa raha hai, jo chaar bright landing lights se roshan hai. Woh taqriban 1,000 feet upar se bohat tez raftar se guzra. Phir us ne engine ki kharabi ka bataya. Aakhir mein us ne kaha: It's not an aircraft. Is ke baad radio par metallic scraping awazein aayin, aur phir mukammal khamoshi. Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.
shorts.descriptionEn:
On 21 October 1978, 20-year-old pilot Frederick Valentich radioed Melbourne about an unknown aircraft over Bass Strait.
His last words were "It's not an aircraft" before the line went silent.

shorts.titleEn: Did Valentich Fear UFOs Before He Vanished?
shorts.text: کیا ایک pilot کو پہلے ہی UFO کا ڈر تھا؟ Frederick Valentich کے والد Guido کے مطابق، وہ UFOs پر پختہ یقین رکھتا تھا۔ والد نے یہ بھی بتایا کہ وہ اس بات سے پریشان رہتا تھا کہ کہیں UFOs اس پر حملہ نہ کر دیں۔ یہ اکیلا بیان نہیں ہے۔ اس کی girlfriend Rhonda Rushton کے مطابق، گمشدگی سے 6 دن پہلے Valentich نے اس سے بات کی تھی کہ شاید کوئی UFO اسے اپنے ساتھ لے جائے۔ یاد رکھیں، یہ دونوں باتیں والد اور girlfriend کے بیانات ہیں۔ دوسری طرف، Department of Transport کو شک تھا کہ UFO اس گمشدگی کے پیچھے تھا۔ کچھ officials کا اندازہ تھا کہ شاید اس نے پانی میں اپنی ہی lights کا عکس دیکھا۔ تو اصل میں کیا ہوا تھا؟ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: Kya ek pilot ko pehle hi UFO ka darr tha? Frederick Valentich ke walid Guido ke mutabiq, woh UFOs par pakka yaqeen rakhta tha. Walid ne yeh bhi bataya ke woh is baat se pareshan rehta tha ke kahin UFOs is par hamla na kar dein. Yeh akela bayan nahin hai. Is ki girlfriend Rhonda Rushton ke mutabiq, gumshudgi se 6 din pehle Valentich ne is se baat ki thi ke shayad koi UFO use apne sath le jaye. Yaad rakhein, yeh donon baatein walid aur girlfriend ke bayanat hain. Doosri taraf, Department of Transport ko shak tha ke UFO is gumshudgi ke peechay tha. Kuch officials ka andaza tha ke shayad us ne pani mein apni hi lights ka aks dekha. To asal mein kya hua tha? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.
shorts.descriptionEn:
Frederick Valentich's father and girlfriend described his belief in UFOs before he disappeared.
Officials, however, were sceptical that a UFO was behind it.

shorts.titleEn: A Piece of Valentich's Plane Washed Ashore 5 Years Later?
shorts.text: پانچ سال بعد سمندر نے ایک چھوٹا سا سراغ لوٹایا۔ 21 October 1978 کو 20 سال کا Frederick Valentich Bass Strait کے اوپر غائب ہو گیا۔ 25 October 1978 کو تلاش بغیر نتیجے کے ختم ہوئی۔ پھر 5 سال بعد Flinders Island کے ساحل پر ایک engine cowl flap بہہ کر آ گیا۔ July 1983 میں Bureau of Air Safety Investigation نے Royal Australian Navy Research Laboratory سے پوچھا کہ کیا یہ حصہ اس علاقے سے بہہ کر آ سکتا ہے۔ Bureau نے بتایا کہ یہ Cessna 182 کا حصہ ہے، اور اس کے serial numbers کی range میں Valentich کا جہاز بھی شامل تھا۔ لیکن اس سے یہ ثابت نہیں ہوتا کہ جہاز کے ساتھ کیا ہوا۔ Department of Transport کی investigation بھی وجہ طے نہ کر سکی۔ تو جواب کہاں ہے؟ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: Paanch saal baad samandar ne ek chhota sa suraagh lauta diya. 21 October 1978 ko 20 saal ka Frederick Valentich Bass Strait ke upar ghayab ho gaya. 25 October 1978 ko talaash baghair nateejay ke khatam hui. Phir 5 saal baad Flinders Island ke sahil par ek engine cowl flap beh kar aa gaya. July 1983 mein Bureau of Air Safety Investigation ne Royal Australian Navy Research Laboratory se poocha ke kya yeh hissa is ilaqay se beh kar aa sakta hai. Bureau ne bataya ke yeh Cessna 182 ka hissa hai, aur is ke serial numbers ki range mein Valentich ka jahaz bhi shamil tha. Lekin is se yeh sabit nahin hota ke jahaz ke sath kya hua. Department of Transport ki investigation bhi wajah tay na kar saki. To jawab kahan hai? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.
shorts.descriptionEn:
Five years after Valentich vanished, an engine cowl flap from a Cessna 182 washed ashore on Flinders Island.
It matched a serial number range that included his aircraft, but the cause remained undetermined.
